forms.label: Reporting a friend's stated preference
forms.japanese: カミラは安くて早い昼食がいいと言っていました。
forms.english: Camila said she wanted a cheap, quick lunch.
forms.explanation: The particle と marks the quoted content, and 言っていました is the polite past of 言っている, used here to report what Camila said earlier. Inside the quote, 安くて is the te-form of the adjective 安い, joining it to 早い so that 安くて早い (cheap and quick) together modify 昼食 (lunch). 〜がいい (X is good/preferred) expresses preference, with が marking the preferred item.

forms.label: Citing the receptionist as the source
forms.japanese: 受付係のイェセニアさんによると、ラーメン店は今満席です。
forms.english: According to receptionist Yesenia, the ramen shop is full now.
forms.explanation: によると means “according to” and attributes the statement to Yesenia. It can appear with a hearsay ending, but this exact card ends in plain です. 受付係のイェセニアさん links her job title and name: “Yesenia, the receptionist.” 満席 means all seats are occupied, and 今 marks the current situation.

forms.label: Proposing a compromise with a question
forms.japanese: 今日は定食にして、明日早めにラーメンを食べませんか。
forms.english: How about a set lunch today and ramen early tomorrow?
forms.explanation: 〜にして is the て-form of 〜にする, “to choose or make it”; it links today’s set lunch to the suggested plan for tomorrow. The polite negative question 食べませんか invites the group to eat ramen tomorrow. 早めに makes 早め (“somewhat early”) an adverb, and を marks ラーメン as the object of 食べる.

speakingObjectives: Report Camila’s limit of 1,500 yen today and her wish for a cheap, quick lunch as hers. Use the exact reporting card: カミラは安くて早い昼食がいいと言っていました。
Report Joaquín's wish for the well-reviewed ramen as his, not yours, e.g., ホアキンは評判のラーメンを食べたいと言っていました。

Attribute Yesenia’s information to her: the ramen shop is full at noon with a line; it is a forty-minute walk and the subway is faster; the near-station set lunch is 1,200 yen with miso soup and tea; the ramen shop opens at 11:30 tomorrow, and arriving before then makes the line easier. Use the exact card: 受付係のイェセニアさんによると、ラーメン店は今満席です。

Propose a set lunch today and ramen early tomorrow, then, after hearing both friends' responses, confirm that the group agrees, e.g., first 今日は定食にして、明日早めにラーメンを食べませんか。 and, once Camila and Joaquín have answered, それなら、みんな賛成ですか。

forms.label: Sequence stops with まず…、それから…
forms.japanese: まずパン屋に行って、それからシャワルマの店に行きましょう。
forms.english: First we will go to the bakery, then to the shawarma shop.
forms.explanation: まず introduces the first stop and それから introduces the next. 行って is the te-form of 行く, linking the first action to the next. 行きましょう is literally a suggestion ("let's go"); the English here renders it as the group's plan.

forms.label: Time promise with 十分以内
forms.japanese: 十分以内に何か食べられるようにします。約束します。
forms.english: I will get us something to eat within ten minutes. I promise.
forms.explanation: 十分以内 means "within ten minutes" and sets the time frame. 食べられる is the potential form of 食べる ("can eat"). ～ようにします means "I will make sure that ~," so the speaker commits to making sure the group can eat something. 約束します means "I promise."

forms.label: Closure state with ～まで閉まっています
forms.japanese: 厨房は十八時まで閉まっています。
forms.english: The kitchen is closed until six.
forms.explanation: ～まで marks the end point of a period, here "until six" (十八時, 18:00). 閉まっています combines the intransitive verb 閉まる ("to close") with ている to describe the current state: it is closed now.

speakingObjectives: Open with your tired, hungry friends: tell them to sit and wait here in the shade and say you will be right back (ここで日陰に座って待っていて。すぐ戻るね。).

Ask Paco whether you can still get something to eat (まだ何か食べられますか。). After he says the kitchen is closed until six, listen for the bakery two streets away and the shawarma shop across from it; ask when that shop closes and whether it has falafel too.
Back with the group, give an ordered plan: first the bakery, then the shawarma shop across from it (まずパン屋に行って、それからシャワルマの店に行きましょう。). Promise food within ten minutes (十分以内に何か食べられるようにします。約束します。).
Tell Ana you will buy her a chocolate pastry at the bakery (アナにはパン屋でチョコレートパンを買うね。), encourage the tired group to keep going together (みんな疲れていますが、一緒に行きましょう。), and close with まず食べて、それから座って休みましょう。

forms.label: Polite request to the grandmother
forms.japanese: おばあさま、このだしの作り方を教えていただけますか。
forms.english: Grandmother, could you tell me how to make this broth?
forms.explanation: おばあさま is お + ばあ + さま, a more formal version of おばあさん. It is a respectful way to address or refer to someone else's grandmother. It is not built from the card term 祖母: 祖母 is how a speaker refers to their own grandmother when talking to outsiders, it is not used to address anyone, and Daniel could not call Eliana 祖母. 作り方 is 作り (the ます-stem of 作る, to make) plus 方 (way of doing). 教えていただけますか is 教えて (te-form of 教える, to teach/tell) + いただく (humble verb for receiving a favor) in its potential form いただける, made polite as いただけます, plus the question marker か. The line is in polite です／ます style, and the humble ～ていただく is a layer of keigo inside that polite style, not a separate third register. In the source this style is used with the grandmother, not with the cousin.

forms.label: Casual request to the cousin (Matías)
forms.japanese: マティアス、パンを取ってくれる？
forms.english: Matías, can you pass me the bread?
forms.explanation: 取って is the te-form of 取る (to take or pick up). くれる is the plain non-past form of the auxiliary meaning that someone does something for the speaker, so 取ってくれる asks for a favor in plain style. The ？ shows rising intonation, which makes the plain form a question. There is no ます and no か, so this is casual speech. Addressing Matías by name without さん also fits the casual style Daniel uses with him in the Reader.

forms.label: Casual request to Valentina
forms.japanese: ヴァレンティナ、もう少し焼きおにぎりをもらってもいい？
forms.english: Valentina, may I have another grilled rice ball?
forms.explanation: The permission pattern is ～てもいい: te-form + the particle も ('even if') + いい ('fine'). Here it is もらって (te-form of もらう, to receive) + も + いい, literally 'is it fine even if I receive'. Only いい is the plain adjective; も is a separate particle. Plain いい with rising intonation (？) and no か makes the question casual. The polite version is もらってもいいですか. もう少し literally means 'a little more'; the source English renders it as 'another' (see reviewNotes). The source shows Valentina inviting casual speech with 「うちでは気楽に話してね。」; reading that as the reason plain style fits this line is an inference, not a source statement.

speakingObjectives: As the guest, open with the source opening, asking エリアナさん whether you may speak to her politely: 「エリアナさん、よかったら、丁寧な言葉でお話ししてもいいですか。」
Ask the grandmother, addressed as おばあさま, for the broth recipe in polite style with a humble request: 「おばあさま、このだしの作り方を教えていただけますか。」
Switch to casual speech with the cousin and then with Valentina: ask Matías to pass the bread with 「マティアス、パンを取ってくれる？」, then ask Valentina for more grilled rice ball with 「ヴァレンティナ、もう少し焼きおにぎりをもらってもいい？」
Close with the source closure, polite thanks said after dessert when Daniel turns to Eliana: 「とてもおいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。」
